clinicalPearls: Instability of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon results from disruption of its fibro-osseous subsheath within the groove on the distal ulna.
Patients report a painful snap over the ulnar wrist, provoked by forearm supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation.
The tendon subluxates volarly and ulnarly out of its groove during supination and relocates on pronation.
Dynamic ultrasound during active supination and pronation is the investigation of choice to demonstrate the subluxation.
Acute subsheath injury may be treated with immobilisation in pronation and slight extension, whereas chronic cases often require subsheath reconstruction.
It is a frequently overlooked cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain, especially in racquet and stick sports.
Because the extensor carpi ulnaris also acts as a dynamic stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint, instability may coexist with DRUJ symptoms.
reference.pathophysiology: The extensor carpi ulnaris occupies the sixth dorsal compartment, held within a groove on the dorsal-ulnar aspect of the distal ulna by a dedicated fibro-osseous subsheath that is distinct from the overlying extensor retinaculum. Forceful or repetitive supination, palmar flexion and ulnar deviation stress this subsheath, and a tear allows the tendon to escape the groove and snap over the ulnar border. Because the subsheath does not readily heal once torn or attenuated, instability tends to become recurrent, and chronic subluxation can produce tendon degeneration and tenosynovitis.
additionalDifferentials: Extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or tenosynovitis
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic ultrasound during active supination and pronation
MRI showing the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon displaced from its groove
Plain radiographs to assess the ulnar groove and exclude bony pathology
MR arthrography if a concomitant TFCC injury is suspected
Comparison examination of the contralateral wrist
Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration of the sixth compartment
redFlags: Locking or fixed dislocation of the tendon
Progressive tendon degeneration or attritional rupture
Failure to improve after appropriate immobilisation
reference.prognosis: Acute injuries immobilised appropriately can settle, while chronic symptomatic subluxation generally responds well to subsheath reconstruction with return to sport in most patients.
pitfalls: Attributing the snapping solely to a TFCC tear and missing tendon instability.
Relying on static imaging, which may appear normal when the tendon is reduced.
Immobilising acutely in the wrong forearm position, such as supination rather than pronation.
Overlooking the tendon's role in distal radioulnar joint stability.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Acute subsheath injury: immobilise the wrist in pronation with slight extension in a cast or splint to allow the fibro-osseous subsheath to heal
Activity modification with avoidance of provocative supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation
Analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and associated tenosynovitis
Chronic or recurrent instability: surgical subsheath reconstruction or stabilisation of the sixth compartment
Address any concomitant triangular fibrocartilage complex injury at the time of treatment
Graduated rehabilitation and staged return to sport after immobilisation or surgery
Refer to hand and wrist surgery for persistent or recurrent subluxation
